tier_reason: These are first-party numbers from Bodo's own repo. The per-system scripts are public (benchmarks/nyc_taxi/bodo/, benchmarks/nyc_taxi/polars/, benchmarks/nyc_taxi/daft/), and the README gives the instance type (r6i.16xlarge) and package versions. But results appear only as PNG bar charts, and no CPU model, compiler or flags are stated, so this falls short of A. It is not an independent suite, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Measured with the Bodo JIT path (run_bodo.py --use_jit), not the Bodo DataFrames pandas API. Single r6i.16xlarge (Mar 2025): Bodo 27.71s vs Polars 282.34s (~10.2x) and vs Daft 69.59s (~2.5x). 4x r6i.16xlarge (Dec 2024): Bodo 17s vs PySpark 389s, Dask 915s and Modin+Ray 4155s; the chart labels these 20x / 50x / 250x, while the README text says '20-240x'. 4 nodes vs Daft (Mar 2025): 17.54s vs 37.78s (~2x). The same README's laptop-scale table shows the Bodo DataFrames API slower than Polars: 5.63s vs 1.244s, and 10.221s vs 4.744s on ~20M rows (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: NYC Taxi FHVHV 'monthly trips with precipitation': the 1,036,465,968-row / 24-column Parquet dataset (24.7 GiB, read from S3) is joined with the 5,538-row Central Park weather CSV. A per-row Python UDF assigns hour-of-day buckets, then the job groups by count and mean trip_miles, sorts, and writes Parquet. The README says 'average trip duration', but the code aggregates trip distance. Single-node run on one AWS r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM).
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (Bodo's own repo), not an independent suite, and numbers are read from bar-chart PNGs rather than a raw results table. The charts measure the Bodo JIT path: the main README carries a 'TODO: updated graph with Taxi benchmark including Bodo DataFrames Pandas API', and the benchmark README's laptop table shows the Bodo DataFrames API slower than Polars (5.63s vs 1.244s; 10.221s vs 4.744s). The Polars implementation buckets hours with map_elements and a Python UDF (row-by-row Python over ~1B rows), which Bodo JIT compiles to native code, so the ~10x single-node gap largely reflects a non-idiomatic Polars baseline. Bodo ran on the Bodo Platform with a forked Arrow for faster Parquet reads. The package table lists bodo 2025.8.2 while the charts date from Dec 2024 / Mar 2025. No compiler/flags are given, and the CPU is identified only by instance type. The single-node comparison excludes pandas.

notes: The numbers match the PNGs exactly, but they belong to Bodo JIT, not the 'Bodo DataFrames' API the record is named after. The repo's own small-scale table has Bodo DataFrames losing to Polars. Consider renaming the entry to Bodo (JIT) or at least keeping the caveat. The last commit is 2026-09-25T18:10Z (pushed_at is 2026-09-26). License is Apache-2.0, 380 stars, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: ClickBench is a well-known public suite. Its harness (ClickHouse/ClickBench chdb-dataframe/, pandas/, polars-dataframe/) runs every system through the same CI on c6a.metal and publishes raw per-query JSON, and chDB beats pandas there by a wide margin. It is not A because no CPU model, compiler or flags are stated (prebuilt pip wheels). Independence is also only partial, since ClickBench is maintained by ClickHouse Inc. and chDB is a ClickHouse derivative.

corrections.benchmark_url: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/tree/main/chdb-dataframe (current raw results: chdb-dataframe/results/20260816/c6a.metal.json vs pandas/results/20260824/c6a.metal.json and polars-dataframe/results/20260824/c6a.metal.json; the README image https://github.com/chdb-io/chdb/raw/main/docs/_static/df_bench.png is an Oct-2024 snapshot)
corrections.claimed_speedup: The README screenshot (committed 2024-10-17) of the ClickBench DataFrame view on c6a.metal shows relative time chDB x1.35, DuckDB x1.40, Polars x9.99 and Pandas x71.18, i.e. ~53x vs Pandas and ~7.4x vs Polars. Current ClickBench raw results on c6a.metal, as the sum of hot-run times (min of runs 2-3) over 43 queries: chDB (DataFrame, 2026-08-16) 6.00s vs pandas (2026-08-24) 2430.31s (~405x) and Polars (DataFrame, 2026-08-24) 11.92s (~2.0x). The latest DuckDB (DataFrame) c6a.metal run (2025-10-09) totals 9.57s (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The README image is an Oct-2024 snapshot. Current ClickBench raw results (Aug 2026) show the Polars gap shrinking from ~7.4x to ~2x, while the pandas gap has widened. ClickBench is maintained by ClickHouse Inc. and chDB is built on ClickHouse (its result JSON is tagged 'ClickHouse derivative'), although all DataFrame runs come from the same public CI harness (github-actions). DataFrame mode times queries over an already-loaded in-memory DataFrame, and load time is excluded from the relative score. No compiler/flags are given (prebuilt wheels), and the CPU is identified only by instance type. The ClickBench README says to take cross-system results with a grain of salt.

notes: The screenshot numbers (1.35/1.40/9.99/71.18) match the record exactly, and the latest raw ClickBench JSONs confirm chDB still wins clearly against pandas and Polars. I downgraded from A to B (no compiler/flags/CPU model; the suite is not fully independent of chDB), and replaced the stale screenshot URL with the live raw-results location. The repo is Apache-2.0 with 2,908 stars, last commit 2026-09-23, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: ClickBench, a well-known third-party suite run by ClickHouse Inc. (Umbra's competitor), measures Umbra against ClickHouse on the same c6a.4xlarge with the public harness (ClickHouse/ClickBench umbra/, clickhouse/, lib/benchmark-common.sh) via its CI. Umbra is closed-source and runs from a prebuilt Docker image (umbradb/umbra:26.09), so compiler/flags are unknown and it cannot be A.

corrections.benchmark_url: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/blob/main/umbra/results/20260918/c6a.4xlarge.json (baselines in the same repo: clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json and duckdb/results/20260511/c6a.4xlarge.json)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Sum of hot-run times (min of runs 2-3, identical to best-of-3 here) over all 43 ClickBench queries: Umbra (2026-09-18, image 26.09) 7.41s vs ClickHouse (2026-09-26 run) 18.03s (~2.4x) and vs DuckDB (2026-05-11 run) 26.25s (~3.5x). Umbra is faster than ClickHouse on 40 of 43 queries. Cold-run sums are 47.27s vs 114.19s (ClickHouse) and 115.19s (DuckDB). 0 failed queries (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: No public source code. ClickBench's CI runs the closed-source binary from the vendor's prebuilt Docker image (umbradb/umbra:26.09), so compiler/flags are not stated. ClickHouse is re-run daily and its hot sum varies (18.00-18.81s over 2026-09-24..26). The ClickBench README warns that direct comparison across systems is tricky and says to take results with a grain of salt. In the supplementary concurrent-QPS test, Umbra's result records concurrent_error_ratio 0.547 (vs 0.001 for ClickHouse).

notes: All three sums re-derive exactly from the raw JSONs (Umbra 7.41 from 20260918, ClickHouse 18.03 from 20260926, DuckDB 26.25 from 20260511). The baseline numbers are in sibling result files, not in the Umbra JSON itself, so I extended benchmark_url. ClickBench flags the entry proprietary: yes, so license is set to 'proprietary'. has_code=false and usability=reference are correct.
